title: All Means All
author: Samantha Lippert
summary: Samantha Lippert reflects on the All Means All! conference in Buffalo and takes away one message: teaching literacy is hard work, but it is not complicated, and schools are stuck on implementation rather than knowledge. She traces her own path from a BOCES Science of Reading symposium, through quiet classroom changes made while she was the only teacher in her building doing so, to a session with Angie Hanlin that confirmed her direction. Her third-grade team then simplified their Wonders basal curriculum, deciding which resources supported the five pillars of literacy, slowing the scope and sequence, and teaching routines explicitly. The results she reports are a median of 156 percent of typical annual growth on i-Ready from fall to winter, state ELA proficiency rising from 51 to 63 percent while the state fell, and math proficiency rising from 57 to 88 percent. She closes with a picture of connected dots to argue that schools over-complicate, and that student outcomes should be the North Star guiding instruction.
points: Lippert's thesis is that schools know what works in literacy and fail at implementation, so the fix is simplification rather than another program.
Her team treated the basal curriculum as a menu: they kept the resources that served the five pillars, dropped others, and built materials for the weak spots.
Explicit routines repeated week after week and a slower scope and sequence gave students time to build comprehension from the text.
She reports concrete gains, including a third grade that moved from 3 points below to 20 points above the state ELA average in one year.
The change took until the January benchmarks to show evidence, which she frames as the point where leaders must trust the process and resist reverting.
quotes: This is the part that I think most schools are stuck at: implementation. It seems so simple and easy, yet comes with so many challenges for schools at the same time.

Change is difficult. It is uncomfortable. But schools have gotten really good at over-complicating things, and I believe the answer to a lot of the challenges schools face currently, is to stop over-complicating things.
Student outcomes and learning need to become our North Star. We need to let the evidence of learning guide our instruction.
We needed to simplify our instruction and stop trying to do everything that our Wonders bloated basal curriculum gave us to do.
Whenever you are making a significant change to something, you have to give it time to make an impact, and resist the urge to go back to old practices.
From fall to winter, my class reached a median of 156% of typical annual growth on the i-Ready Reading Diagnostic, about three times the expected pace for that window.
In other words our 3rd grade went from 3 points below the state average to now 20 points above the state average in one school year.
We removed the over-complicated and overwhelmed feeling for both the teachers and the students. We do what actually works and we do it over and over again. Day after day, week after week.
context: Lippert locates the literacy problem in implementation, not in missing knowledge.
She argues that complexity, not difficulty, is what stalls schools.
Learning evidence, not programs, is meant to steer instructional decisions.
Her team pruned the basal curriculum to what served the pillars of literacy.
Real change needs time before results appear, so consistency matters.
Mid-year benchmark growth gave the first hard evidence that the changes worked.
State test results are offered as proof that the simplified approach outperformed the trend.
Simplicity is presented as a relief for both teachers and students.
